newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr settles in mid-range as rally fades.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr settles in mid-range as rally fades.

text.p: The Australian dollar faded at the midsession after an early attempt at extending an offshore rally foundered on the shoals of US$0.7765 resistance.

The currency had enjoyed a short-covering rally overnight as speculators bought in anticipation of U.S. demand related to the sale of a Victorian power station. However, no actual demand had been seen as yet and there was talk the negotiations had hit a sticking point which could delay announcement of the winner for a few days, making those who were long rather nervous.
Nevertheless, the uncertainty alone might help alleviate the impact of shrinking yield premiums and keep US$0.7720 intact.
By 12.30 pm (0230 GMT) the local currency had relaxed to US$0.7748/53 from an early US$0.7762/67 but was still up on Thursday's late US$0.7720/25.

On the crosses it softened to 97.38/48 yen from an early 97.83/93, partly due to comments from Japanese Ministry of Finance forex guru Eisuke Sakakibara that the yen's weakness was not justified by fundamentals and the U.S. shared its concern over the speed of the recent fall.
He also said it would be dangerous to assume Japanese interest rates would not rise within the next year, as the JGB market seemed to be.
The U.S. dollar also dipped in response to 125.68/73 from 125.95/00 but market expectations the Federal Reserve would hike rates next month kept a solid floor under the currency.
That prospect was not so welcome for A$ bulls since its yeild premium over the U.S. currency had already been whittled away and had actually turned negative for one-year money.

The local dollar has traditionally been thought of as a high yielder so this development was forcing offshore investors to reappraise their whole attitude to the A$ and Australian assets. The result need not be all negative for the A$ since Australia's relative inflation performance had improved markedly.

Consumer price data for the March quarter next week were expected to show a modest rise of around 0.1 percent taking annual CPI growth to 1.2 from 1.5 percent in Q4. That compares to 3.3 percent in the U.S. and if sustained whould make Australia steadily more competitive vs-a-vis the U.S.
The key underlying rate was seen rising around 0.3 percent so slowing annual inflation to 2.0 percent from 2.1.

This would be the very bottom of the Reserve Bank's 2-3 percent target range, possibly providing the scope for the RBA to ease again should the real economy not show the robust recovery it expected. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
